source.title: Pumpout: A Meta Approach for Robustly Training Deep Neural Networks with Noisy Labels
source.authors: Bo Han; Gang Niu; Jiangchao Yao; Xing-Rui Yu; Miao Xu; I. Tsang; Masashi Sugiyama

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own experiments on training with corrupted labels, relevant to V4, but does not reproduce the original random-label experiment or test the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2017) for fitting completely random labels and Arpit et al. (2017) for learning patterns first; those cited findings are not rows. Its own experiments vary label-noise conditions and report test accuracy, but do not report training error for the Table 2 results.
record.test_reason: The study reports ordinary-training baselines that memorize corrupted labels and explicitly identifies patterns-first learning in its own experiments. These bear on V4 and V6, although the extracted rows contain only the proposed mitigation methods' test performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: SIGUA uses underweighted gradient ascent on selected data to robustify self-teaching and backward correction, often improving noisy-label test performance. The authors describe this as trading optimization against generalization and emphasize distinguishing desired from undesired memorization.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes SIGUA and evaluates noisy-label learning methods; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with dataset, corruption type and level, and learning method; the authors also report different outcomes across these settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 reports SIGUASL and SIGUABC test accuracy relative to clean-label supervised learning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Targeted noisy-label mitigation can preserve high test accuracy, sometimes approaching a clean-label supervised comparator.

record.problems: The Table 2 results report test accuracy but not training error, so they cannot establish whether training data were fit perfectly. The experiments use particular noisy-label processes and methods, not completely random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No other own results were extracted: Figures 1–5 report curves, but the text does not provide the condition-specific numerical values needed to record them reliably. Cited results were excluded.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, chance-level testing, and fitting without changing the true-label training recipe.
Training-time overhead relative to true labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases. Comparing wide and deep networks does not test these.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit throughout a corruption sweep from zero to fully random labels, and a steady test-error trajectory toward chance. The directly reported memorization experiment fixes symmetric corruption at 80%.
Controlled tests of weight decay, dropout, or augmentation preventing random-label fitting, and generalization after removing these regularizers.
A complete-random-label comparison and direct quantitative separation of clean-label and noisy-label learning times in the main benchmark experiments.

missing.what: Separate rows for wide and deep networks' perfect memorization under 80% symmetric noise before the intervention: approximately epoch 120 and epoch 60, respectively, with test accuracy about 23%. Although rows_left_out declares Figure 1 curves omitted, its assertion that condition-specific numerical results are unavailable overlooks these explicit textual results.
missing.locator: Section 2, Figure 1 setup and accompanying experimental-results bullets

record.verdict_notes: Figures 2–5 are already declared omitted in rows_left_out; the V6 verdicts rely on the authors' explicit interpretation of their own results, without inventing curve values. Figure 1's ordinary-training phase qualifies as spontaneous memorization under noisy supervision; its later oracle-guided forgetting intervention does not challenge V4 or V6.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels; zero or near-zero training error; test error at chance; unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training time relative to true labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Shuffled pixels, permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Whether training error stays perfect across corruption levels, whether test error rises steadily toward chance, and whether the model captures remaining signal while memorizing noise.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation stop random-label fitting, and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
The paper cites prior work on learning patterns first but does not test whether real and random labels are learned differently over training.

relationships.condition: MNIST with 80% symmetric label flips; ordinary momentum-SGD training during epochs 1–150, for both wide and deep networks.
relationships.reason: Text accompanying Figure 1 reports perfect memorization of intact and flipped training data around epochs 120 and 60, respectively, with test accuracy about 23%. This supports fitting signal plus noise at this corruption level; no extracted row captures it.
relationships.display_finding: Wide and deep networks perfectly memorized intact and flipped training labels around epochs 120 and 60, respectively, while test accuracy was about 23%.

relationships.condition: Standard training on noisy MNIST and CIFAR-10 under symmetry-20%, symmetry-50%, and pair-45%.
relationships.reason: Section 4 explicitly interprets the Figure 2 training trajectories as patterns-first learning, followed by declining test accuracy. This is qualitative temporal evidence from the text; no extracted row captures it.
relationships.display_finding: Training trajectories showed early pattern learning followed by declining test accuracy, which the authors attributed to later noise fitting.

relationships.condition: Backward-corrected training on noisy MNIST and CIFAR-10 under the three tested corruption settings.
relationships.reason: Section 4 explicitly states that BC models also learned patterns first despite loss correction, referring to Figure 3. This is qualitative evidence from the text; no extracted row captures it.
relationships.display_finding: The authors reported that backward-corrected models also learned patterns first despite loss correction.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
